Freely
FREE-ly
adv.
From free and -ly: without cost, without constraint, liberally. Webster 1828: at liberty; without constraint; gratuitously. The word marks the manner of God’s giving from the first command in Eden to the last invitation in Revelation.

Biblical Definition

The first word God speaks to man about the garden is a permission, and it is generous before it is restrictive: Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat (Genesis 2:16). The prohibition follows in the next verse and concerns one tree; the liberty is stated first and covers everything else. That order is worth noticing, because the serpent will invert it in Genesis 3:1. The word then carries the doctrine of justification: Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:24) — the Greek adverb means as a gift, without cause in the recipient, the same word rendered without a cause in John 15:25. Our Lord sets the manner of ministry to match the manner of receiving: freely ye have received, freely give (Matthew 10:8). And Scripture closes with the invitation in the same terms: whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely (Revelation 22:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FREELY as at liberty; without constraint or restraint; without necessity; liberally; generously; gratuitously; without purchase or cost.

expand to see more

FREELY, adv. — At liberty; without vassalage, slavery or dependence.

Without constraint, restraint or compulsion; of one’s own accord.

Plentifully; in abundance; as, to eat freely.

Without scruple or reserve; also, gratuitously, without purchase or cost.

From free, Anglo-Saxon freo, and the adverbial -ly.

Key Scripture

Genesis 2:16 — "And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat:"

Romans 3:24 — "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:"

Matthew 10:8 — "Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give."

Revelation 22:17 — "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely."

Modern Corruption

Romans 3:24 says justification is freely given — as a gift, without cause in the receiver — which is the precise word Rome’s doctrine of infused righteousness and merit cannot accommodate.

expand to see more

The Greek adverb in Romans 3:24 is dorean, meaning as a gift, gratuitously, and the same word is used in John 15:25 for hating Christ without a cause. Justification, then, is without cause in the justified — there is nothing in the sinner that occasions it. This is the exact point of the Reformation controversy. Trent anathematized the doctrine that a man is justified by faith alone and that the righteousness by which he is justified is Christ’s imputed to him rather than his own infused and cooperated with; and the whole apparatus of merit, satisfaction and indulgence follows from denying dorean. The Protestant answer is not that works do not matter but that they are the fruit of justification and never its cause. Grace ceases to be grace the moment a cause in the receiver is admitted (Romans 11:6).

Genesis 2:16 rewards attention for the order in which God speaks. The liberty is announced first and is comprehensive — every tree of the garden — and one prohibition follows. When the serpent opens his mouth in Genesis 3:1 he reverses this: Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden? The first recorded temptation is a misrepresentation of God’s generosity as restriction, and every temptation since has carried some form of the same suggestion, that obedience is a narrowing and God is holding out. The doctrine to hold against it is stated in the same chapter: God gave everything and withheld one thing, and the one thing was withheld for the good of the man who was given all the rest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew akol tokel, an emphatic infinitive absolute, eating thou mayest eat; Greek dorean (G1432), as a gift, gratuitously; charis (G5485), grace.

expand to see more

Hebrew akol tokel — the infinitive absolute doubling the verb for emphasis; thou mayest freely eat (Genesis 2:16).

Greek dorean (G1432) — as a gift, gratuitously, without cause; justified freely by his grace (Romans 3:24).

Greek charis (G5485) — grace, unmerited favour; the companion noun in the same clause.

Greek apolutrosis (G629) — redemption, a ransoming; the means through which the free justification comes.

Greek thelo (G2309) — to will or desire; whosoever will (Revelation 22:17).

Usage

"Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat (Genesis 2:16) — the liberty stated first, and comprehensive."

"Being justified freely by his grace (Romans 3:24) — dorean, without cause in the receiver."

"Freely ye have received, freely give (Matthew 10:8) — the manner of ministry matched to the manner of receiving."
